implementation_notes: Rust has no authorization service, so the trait is the Policy: trait Policy<R> { fn decide(&self, sub: &Subject, act: Action, res: &R) -> Decision; } and the guard is a wrapper function or, in axum, an extractor implementing FromRequestParts that rejects the request before the handler runs (docs.rs: axum::extract). What replaces the classic structure: traits plus wrapper/extractor functions replace the Policy/Guard class pair, and the borrow checker prevents the guard from holding mutable aliases to the resource it protects; the stdlib's RAII guards (MutexGuard) show the same guard idiom used for resources rather than rights. Choose this runtime form when the policy is configured at start-up, data-driven, or must be swapped in tests; take the typestate variant when the compiler should prove that a check happened.
idiom_name: Policy trait + wrapper function / axum extractor
pitfalls: A refreshable policy behind a shared reference must be Send + Sync (or per-request); an internal RwLock held across the operation serialises the whole resource.
unwrap()/expect() on a missing subject or denied decision turns an authorization failure into a panic - a denial-of-service; return Result and map denial at the boundary.
An axum extractor runs for every request it is attached to, but routes that do not declare it are unguarded; consider attaching the guard at the router level and excluding public routes explicitly.

variants.name: typestate capability token (Authorized<R>)
variants.implementation_notes: The Rust-specific realization makes the guard a proof token: the policy module returns Authorized<R> - a newtype holding the resource reference plus a PhantomData marker for lifetime and variance tracking - and protected operations accept only that token, so code that skipped the decision cannot name a value to pass; denial is an Err. What replaces the classic structure: a private constructor and the type system replace the runtime guard call, and the check happens once and is carried in the type. Choose this for intra-process APIs where the compiler should prove authorization; keep the runtime trait form where policy data is dynamic or the decision must be re-evaluated per request.
pitfalls: A pub constructor or pub field defeats the token; keep Authorized::new and its field private to the policy module and audit for accidental re-exports.
PhantomData and variance mistakes let a token outlive the resource reference it proves; tie the lifetime parameter to the resource.
Tokens are in-process proofs, not transferable credentials - they must not be serialized or sent over the wire.
variants.idiom_name: Authorized<R> token constructible only by the policy module
